notes: Scoped to the non-Latin targets a traveller cannot sound out at all. `he` joined with the Hebrew pack, and `hy` with the Armenian one -- which is the point: the cheapest moment to get a scope right is when the language lands, because widening it later changes a shipped language's sheets. Five more belong here on the same reading and are not in it -- hi, th, ru, el and ka -- which is the shape of the Italian-euro omission: the scope is the packs that were ported first, not a decision about which scripts are opaque.

Moved out of quick-responses, which is printed by default: a board answer that reshapes every card is the thing the plan forbids doing silently, and it moved four lines of the reference sheet. The other party's answer to 'How long is the wait?'. Venue-neutral on purpose, so one row serves a restaurant, a clinic, a ticket desk and a spa instead of a copy per board. Two clauses rather than one: a bare negative can be heard as 'do not wait here' or as a brush-off, and the second clause is the permission to proceed that makes it an answer.
Permission, not existence; 'Do you have Wi-Fi?' already exists in the corpus.
ID registration is required for local SIMs in well over 100 countries; expect a passport scan.
Shop staff normally insert and activate the SIM before you leave.
Written beats spoken: the password is a string, not a word.
Slot is a place name; asked before heading somewhere remote.
Often kept as the Latin abbreviation; give the local form only if one is really used.
Deliberately general: point at anything and ask.
Must stay a neutral yes/no question. Verified that tipping is not customary and can be unwelcome in Japan, China and South Korea, so never render this as 'how much should I tip?'.
Asks whether a service charge is already on the bill.
Asking permission at a threshold: temple, shrine, shop, home.
Asks a person's consent to be photographed. Distinct from attractions-tickets.may-i-take-photos, which is about the place.
Slot is a place or service. Gloss uses 'queue' to match trail-transport.how-long-is-the-queue; US English is 'line'.
Asks whether the traveler's clothing is acceptable here, e.g. at a religious site.
An apology for an unintended breach of custom. Should read as sincere, not defensive.
Open question about the local norm; it presupposes nothing, which is the point. Used after etiquette.is-tipping-expected.
Only useful where tipping is customary; kept at low importance for that reason. Do not treat as the default way to pay.

SAFETY-CRITICAL. Means the child is missing right now and help is needed immediately. Must NOT be rendered with any idiom that can mean bereavement (English 'I lost my child' has that reading, which is why this wording was chosen). Requires a fluent-speaker check.
Asks staff to page the child over a public-address system. Pairs with children.cannot-find-my-child.
Slot is a number of years. Doubles as the answer to an age limit and as identifying detail for a missing child.
A raised feeding chair for a small child in a restaurant.
Chosen over 'Where can I change my baby?', which is ambiguous. Matches international signage (baby changing / nursing room).
Asks the lowest age allowed to enter or ride.
Asks whether children are charged at all, which is the useful question where child fares vary.
US 'crib' = UK 'cot'. Means a baby bed provided in a hotel room.
A baby's feeding bottle. Warm, not boil.
A child restraint seat for a car; say 'child car seat' so it is not read as an ordinary vehicle seat.
US 'stroller' / UK 'pram, pushchair'. Reference word for signage and for pointing.

One line of prose in the reader's own language about a property of Thai that no phrase row can carry. The pack deliberately omits the sentence-final politeness particles from 743 of its 745 rows, because printing both correctly needs two different pairs -- ค่ะ on a statement, คะ on a question -- and picking one is wrong for half its readers. This is the legend that makes that decision work.

Generalises massage-spa.reply-none-of-these into a universal, unscoped fallback so every reply set can use one row rather than borrowing one scoped to zh-Hans and filed under massage. Required in every reply set, exactly as the row it replaces was.
The spoken answer, distinct from the bare signage word common-signs.closed / trail-warnings.closed.
The shopkeeper's or kitchen's negative answer to shopping.do-you-have-this-in-stock and similar questions; venue-neutral like there-is-no-wait.

Clustered with there-is-no-wait as the other half of the same wait topic. Worded 'One moment, please' rather than communication.please-wait-a-moment's 'Please wait a moment', both for a distinct staff-service register and to drop the second-person imperative 'wait', which is gendered in several languages a supplied reply must stay neutral for.

The other party offering to lead the traveller there, distinct from the static location answer it-is-over-there. Written without a second-person object ('the way', not 'you') so the reply carries no addressee gender where an object pronoun would mark one.
The complete clarifying question staff actually ask; question-words.how-many is the bare reference word for that section's glossary, not a usable reply.
A natural spoken refusal, distinct from quick-responses.cannot-not-possible, which is a bare slash-form word for the traveller's own quick response rather than a reply someone gives back.
Worded as the verbless 'One more time, please?' rather than a direct imperative, which would be a second-person form gendered in several languages a supplied reply must stay neutral for.
The other party's offer, distinct from communication.please-write-it-down, which is the traveller's own request in the other direction.

The bystander's own announcement, first person from the listener's side, not the traveller's -- distinct from emergency-medical.please-call-an-ambulance, which is the traveller's request that someone else place the call.

Textually identical to the traveller's own police-consulate.i-am-calling-the-police, but said by the other party as a reassurance rather than a self-defence assertion in a dispute -- kept separate for the reason board-answers.it-is-closed is kept separate from common-signs.closed: a board answer is a different speech act from the phrase it echoes, even where the words match.
A general reassurance that does not name which service was called, so one row covers the ambulance, the police or a bystander already acting.

The other party's diagnostic question, distinct from emergency-medical.it-hurts-here, which is the traveller's own statement, and from massage-spa.reply-does-it-hurt-there, which points at one area already named in a massage context rather than asking generally.

Worded as the impersonal 'Is walking possible?' rather than 'Can you walk?', a direct second-person question that is gendered in Arabic, Hebrew, Polish and the Indo-Aryan languages -- see content/PROMPTS/speaker-variants.md. Mandarin has no such hazard, so its row addresses the traveller directly with 您.

Worded as the nominal 'Staying here is best' rather than the imperative 'Stay here', which out-genders the traveller in the same languages as can-you-walk. Distinct from lost-rescue.we-are-here, which is the traveller's own statement of location, not an instruction received from someone else.

Worded as 'What is the name?' rather than 'What is your name?' to drop the second-person possessive, for the reason given at can-you-walk and stay-here. Distinct from introductions.what-is-your-name, which is peer register between two travellers meeting casually; this concept is a stranger addressing someone in distress, and its Mandarin row uses 您 rather than the 你 the introductions row already carries.
A bystander's reassurance of proximity, distinct from emergency-medical.where-is-the-nearest-hospital, which is the traveller's own question.
Explains why the other party cannot simply hand back a phone or read out a number, and why they may need to act themselves rather than direct the traveller to call.

The bystander's fallback when they cannot help further themselves -- finding staff, a doctor or anyone else able to, rather than a specific promise like i-am-calling-an-ambulance or i-am-calling-the-police.
